title: Lesson 8: Marriage and Relationships
description: Every close relationship runs on either a contract or a covenant. Through the story of Ruth and Naomi, you will see the promise-keeping love God shows you first, and how that same covenant love can shape a marriage, a friendship, and every season of life, married or single.

blocks.text: You have spent this course learning to love outward: your neighbors, your family at home, your church family, and the people your gifts can bless. This lesson looks at the love that holds your closest relationships together. It is called covenant love, and it starts with the way God has already loved you.

blocks.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
blocks.text:
Long ago, during a famine, a woman named Naomi moved with her husband and two sons from Bethlehem to the land of Moab. There her husband died. Her sons married two women from Moab named Orpah and Ruth, and about ten years later both sons died too (Ruth 1:3-5). Three widows were left grieving, with their husbands gone and their future uncertain.

Naomi decided to go home to Bethlehem. She told her daughters-in-law to go back to their own families, where they would have a better chance at a future. Orpah kissed her goodbye and went, but Ruth held on to her.

Ruth had every reason to leave. Naomi told her plainly that she had no more sons to give her (Ruth 1:11-13). Still, Ruth made a promise: "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God." (Ruth 1:16).

Ruth walked into a foreign land with a grieving old woman, gathered leftover grain in the fields to feed them both, and kept her word. God saw it. He brought a faithful man named Boaz into her life, who treated Ruth with kindness and honor and later married her. Their great-grandson was King David, and from David's family line came Jesus (Ruth 4:17; Matthew 1:5).

Ruth's words are often read at weddings, but she first spoke them to her widowed mother-in-law. That is worth noticing, because Ruth was not falling in love. She was keeping faith. The book of Ruth uses a Hebrew word for this kind of love, hesed, which means loyal, steadfast, promise-keeping love (Ruth 1:8; 3:10). It is love that says, "I will stay," when leaving would be easier.

Before covenant love is something you give, it is something you receive. God is the first and most faithful promise keeper. When His people broke their promises again and again, He kept His. At the cross, Jesus showed how far God's faithful love would go. He paid for your sin, and you can trust Him to keep His promises.
The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
8.1 - Ruth stayed when leaving would have been easier. Who has shown you that kind of faithful, staying love, and how did it help you see what God's love is like?
Contract or Covenant?

Every close relationship runs on one of two kinds of agreement. A contract says, "I will, if you will." It is built on performance. As long as you keep your side, I will keep mine, and when you stop meeting my needs, I am free to go. A covenant says, "I will, even when." It is built on a promise. I will keep my word even on the days you are hard to love, because my faithfulness rests on my promise, not on your performance.

Contracts are not wrong. You sign one when you rent an apartment or take a job. But a contract cannot carry the weight of a marriage, a lifelong friendship, or a church family, because people are not services. When love is only a contract, it lasts until the first real disappointment.

blocks.alt: Diagram: a contract says I will, if you will, and ends when needs stop. A covenant says I will, even when, and holds on hard days. Underneath, God keeps covenant with you first.

blocks.text: Here is the good news in this picture. You cannot give covenant love just by trying harder. You give it because you have received it. God never related to you on a contract. If He had, you would have been out long ago. Jesus called His death the "new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). Covenant love flows out of you after it has flowed into you.

blocks.title: What covenant love is not
content: Covenant love is patient with ordinary weakness and ordinary hard days. It is not a promise to stay in danger. God never asks you to accept abuse, threats, or control, or to cover for someone who is hurting you or your children. Keeping your promises does not make you responsible for another person's sin.

If someone is harming, threatening, or controlling you, please tell a pastor or another safe, trusted person and get help. If you are in immediate danger, call 911. In the United States you can also call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

blocks.text: 8.2 - Think of one close relationship in your life. Where do you tend to treat it like a contract, "I will, if you will"? What would "I will, even when" look like there?
Marriage: A Living Picture of the Gospel

God designed marriage to be the clearest human picture of covenant love. From the very beginning, a husband and wife were meant to leave their parents, hold fast to each other, and become one. Paul shows the secret behind that design.
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.

A mystery in the Bible is something God kept hidden for a while and then revealed. Here is what He revealed: every Christian marriage is a small, daily picture of Jesus and His church. Jesus did not wait for His bride to become lovely before He loved her. He gave Himself for her while she was still wandering. So a Christian marriage is not two perfect people who finally found each other. It is two imperfect people held by a faithful God, choosing to love each other the way Jesus loves them.

Most days, covenant love in marriage looks ordinary. It sounds like, "I was wrong. Will you forgive me?" It looks like yielding, choosing to serve when you would rather be served, and staying kind in the middle of a disagreement. At its best, marriage gives a rare gift: someone sees you at your worst and keeps choosing you anyway. Being fully known and still loved is a small picture of how God loves you in Jesus. Marriage is a blessing, but it is not your ultimate satisfaction. Only Jesus can carry that weight.

8.3 - If you are married, what is one ordinary way you could show your spouse covenant love? If you are not married right now, what have you seen in a healthy marriage that shows you something true about how Jesus loves His church?
Every Season Can Be Faithful

Maybe you are single and hoping to marry. Maybe you are single and content to stay that way. Maybe you are divorced, or your spouse has died, or your marriage is hard right now. God does not treat any of these seasons as a waiting room. Jesus Himself never married, and He lived the most complete human life ever lived.
The apostle Paul, who was also unmarried, called singleness a gift, not a lesser life.
I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.

Paul even said an unmarried person can have a special freedom for "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). Covenant love is not only for husbands and wives. It shows up in faithful friendships and in the way you keep showing up for your church family. You can see it in Ruth, who kept faith with Naomi long before she ever met Boaz.
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.

If you are carrying grief or regret about marriage, hear this clearly: your worth is not measured by your relationship status. Whether you are married, single, divorced, or widowed, God fully knows you and fully loves you. There is a faithful way to live in the season you are in right now.
8.4 - What is hard about the season of life you are in right now? What would it look like to trust that God can make this season a place of faithfulness instead of a waiting room?
Lesson 8 Review

Ruth kept faith with Naomi when leaving would have been easier, and God wove her faithfulness into the story of Jesus. That is covenant love. A contract says, "I will, if you will," but a covenant says, "I will, even when." You can give that kind of love because God gave it to you first in Jesus. Marriage is one beautiful picture of it, and every season of life is a place to practice it. In the next lesson, you will see how purity protects these covenant relationships and keeps your heart free.
